writing.exampleCaption: Classification checklist for Copy with Random Links
writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Copy with Random Links when it asks for deep copy of graphs shaped like a list. Here the concrete task is: Return copied values with random target indexes. The visible input `values=[7,13,11] random=[null,0,1]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Look for tasks where node identity or one-way traversal matters. An indexed vector solution can hide the pointer constraint rather than solve it. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Map old nodes to new nodes or interleave copies so arbitrary links can be reconstructed. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A list algorithm changes relationships between nodes, not just values. Draw the next pointers before and after each mutation. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(n) map or O(1) interleaving; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `7:null,13:0,11:1` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check an empty list, one node, a head or tail change, and cycles when the problem allows them. Rust ownership makes linked structures explicit: use the provided node type, take links carefully, and preserve access to the remaining chain. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
